lessons.title: Paper Trading: The Bridge Between Backtest and Real Capital

body.text: The most realistic backtest still runs on historical data through code that has had weeks to be debugged. Paper trading is the first time the actual live pipeline meets a market that is happening right now, and it is where a whole category of bug that backtesting cannot touch finally gets a chance to surface, before any real capital is involved.

children.text: Why a Passed Backtest Still Isn't Enough

Chapter 5 built the most realistic backtest this course will construct: slippage, latency, partial fills, tail-risk metrics, distributional shift monitoring, stress-tested against known historical regimes. All of it still runs on historical data through code that has had every chance to be tested and debugged over weeks of development. Paper trading closes the one gap none of that can touch: running the actual live decision pipeline, real-time data in, model prediction out, against markets that are happening right now, with no real capital at risk while integration problems get found and fixed.
What Paper Trading Actually Tests That Backtesting Cannot

cells: Live, streaming, and occasionally late, missing, or malformed
Whether the strategy and reward design are sound, using clean data as a given
Whether the actual live pipeline, data feed, state construction, order logic, works correctly end to end
Logic errors in the strategy itself
Integration bugs: API timeouts, malformed live data, timing assumptions that only break under real-time conditions
None; it's a simulation of the past
None; simulated or logged decisions against a live feed, without routing real orders

children.text: Building a Minimal Paper Trading Loop

The single most important discipline in building a paper trading loop is reusing the exact same state-construction code the training environment and backtest already used, not writing a second, parallel implementation for live data. Two implementations of the same feature, one for offline data and one for live data, will eventually disagree in some subtle way, a different rolling window boundary, a different way of handling a missing print, a rounding difference, and that disagreement is invisible until it quietly changes what the agent sees at exactly the moment it matters.

body.code:
# Reuses NiftyFuturesEnv._get_state() unchanged, rather than
# reimplementing feature construction separately for live data
from my_broker_api import get_latest_bars  # placeholder for a real broker data feed

shadow_env = NiftyFuturesEnv(price_data=get_latest_bars(lookback_window=10))

while market_is_open():
    latest_bars = get_latest_bars(lookback_window=shadow_env.lookback)
    shadow_env.prices = latest_bars["close"].values
    shadow_env.volumes = latest_bars["volume"].values
    shadow_env.t = len(shadow_env.prices) - 1

    state = shadow_env._get_state()
    action, _ = model.predict(state, deterministic=True)

    log_decision(timestamp=now(), state=state, action=action)  # no real order placed
    wait_for_next_bar()
body.caption: shadow_env reuses the same class, and the same _get_state() method, that trained and backtested the agent. log_decision() records what the agent would have done, for later comparison against what the backtest expected, without ever calling a real order placement function.

children.text: How Long to Paper Trade, and What Would Make You Stop

There is no universally correct paper trading duration. A reasonable floor is long enough to observe a meaningful sample of the agent's actual decisions, not just a handful of trades, and ideally long enough to include at least one stretch of noticeably different volatility, not only a single unusually quiet week that tells you little about how the pipeline behaves under stress. What matters more than the exact duration is deciding the criteria for stopping, and what would count as pass or fail, before paper trading begins, not after seeing how it goes.

body.caption: Deciding Pass/Fail Criteria Before Paper Trading Begins

cells: Paper trading Sharpe within a reasonable range of what the backtest projected for a similar period, not necessarily identical, but not wildly divergent
No unexplained data gaps, timeouts, or state-construction errors during the observation window
The Chapter 5 shift monitor is not firing constantly; frequent flags during a period the backtest treated as unremarkable suggests a live pipeline problem, not a genuine regime shift

body.text: It is worth being precise about a failure mode that looks like distributional shift or market non-stationarity but is neither: train-serve skew, where the live pipeline computes a feature subtly differently than the offline pipeline that trained and backtested the agent did, for reasons that have nothing to do with the market itself changing. A shift-detection flag firing during paper trading could mean a genuine regime shift, exactly what Chapter 5 built it to catch, or it could mean the live and offline code paths have quietly diverged. Reusing identical state-construction code, as this lesson's shadow loop does, is what keeps this specific failure mode from being confused with the ones Chapter 5 already covers.

body.title: Diagnosing Frequent Shift Alerts During Paper Trading
body.scenario: During the first week of paper trading, Chapter 5's distributional shift monitor fires repeatedly, flagging most incoming live states as out-of-distribution, even though the week's market conditions were unremarkable by any conventional measure, no unusual volatility, no news events.
body.prompt: Given what this lesson covered, what would you check first, and why might this not actually indicate a genuine market regime shift?
body.modelAnswer: Given that the week's market conditions were unremarkable, the first thing to check is whether the live state-construction pipeline is computing features identically to the offline pipeline that trained and backtested the agent, comparing a handful of live feature values against what the same underlying price and volume data would have produced through the training environment's own _get_state() method. Frequent flags during an objectively unremarkable week are a strong signal of train-serve skew rather than genuine distributional shift: a subtle difference in how a rolling window boundary is computed, how a missing print is handled, or even a library version difference between the offline training environment and the live pipeline could produce systematically different feature values that look like out-of-distribution states to the shift monitor, without the market itself having done anything unusual at all.

body.title: Why Reuse the Same State-Construction Code
body.question: Why does this lesson insist on reusing the exact same _get_state() method for the live paper trading loop that was used during training and backtesting, rather than writing a separate implementation optimized for live data?
options: Because writing a second implementation is always slower to develop

Because two separate implementations of the same feature logic will eventually diverge in some subtle way, and that divergence, train-serve skew, can silently change what the agent sees at exactly the moment it matters, in a way that is easy to mistake for a genuine market regime shift
Because Stable-Baselines3 requires the exact same function object to be used at both training and inference time
Because live data cannot be processed using the same code as historical data for technical reasons
body.explanation: Train-serve skew, a live pipeline computing a feature subtly differently from the offline pipeline that trained the model, is a real and easy-to-miss failure mode. It produces symptoms, like distributional shift alerts, that look identical to a genuine market regime change, but the cause is a code inconsistency rather than anything happening in the market. Reusing identical state-construction code removes this entire category of risk by construction, rather than relying on careful testing to catch every possible subtle divergence between two implementations.

points: Paper trading validates something backtesting structurally cannot: whether the actual live pipeline, data feed, state construction, model inference, order logic, works correctly against real-time conditions, with no real capital at risk while integration problems get found
The single most important paper trading discipline is reusing the exact same state-construction code used during training and backtesting, rather than a second, parallel implementation for live data

Train-serve skew, a live and offline pipeline quietly computing the same feature differently, produces symptoms that can look identical to genuine distributional shift or market regime change, but the cause is a code inconsistency, not the market
There is no universal paper trading duration, but a reasonable floor covers a meaningful sample of decisions and, ideally, more than one volatility regime, not just a single quiet week

Pass or fail criteria for paper trading need to be decided before it begins, using the same one-touch discipline against peeking and re-deciding that Chapter 4's hyperparameter tuning and Chapter 5's stress-testing both already insisted on
Frequent distributional shift alerts during an otherwise unremarkable period are a signal worth investigating as a possible pipeline bug before being accepted at face value as a genuine regime shift
